content:
Former Liberal minister Philip Ruddock has been appointed by cabinet to review whether Australian law adequately protects the human right to religious freedom. The move follows the same-sex marriage “yes” vote and comes as parliament prepares marriage equality legislation.

The review is partly aimed at heading off a divisive debate over religious protections in the marriage bill. Treasurer Scott Morrison, however, has warned that the review is “no substitute” for inserting religious freedom amendments directly into the same-sex marriage legislation.

Prime minister Malcolm Turnbull said the review is needed to carefully examine religious freedom in light of the impending changes to marriage law. Some senior conservatives, including Peter Dutton and Mathias Cormann, want a separate religious freedom bill considered next year, while others, such as Morrison and Liberal senator David Fawcett, argue it should be dealt with alongside the marriage bill.

Ruddock has been asked to report by 31 March. Turnbull noted that numerous proposals to bolster religious protections have emerged recently, many reaching beyond marriage issues, and he cautioned parliament to be wary of their broader effects.

Turnbull stressed that reforms to protect religious freedom must be handled carefully due to the risk of unintended consequences, especially from broad, bill-of-rights-style measures. He described the review as a “timely expert stocktake” to guide any future legislative changes and said Ruddock was chosen because of his experience as Australia’s special envoy for human rights.
